pure virtual function|pure virtual: A virtual function declared with the pure specifier and no body, `virtual void f() = 0;`. A concrete derived class must override it. See [Pure virtual functions and abstract classes](#/comp3522-w4/abstract-classes).
pure specifier|= 0: The `= 0` after a virtual function's declaration that makes it pure virtual. A declaration cannot have both a pure specifier and a body. See [Pure virtual functions and abstract classes](#/comp3522-w4/abstract-classes).
abstract class: A class with one or more pure virtual functions. It cannot be instantiated, returned by value or taken by value, but pointers and references to it are fine; it may have data members and ordinary functions. See [Pure virtual functions and abstract classes](#/comp3522-w4/abstract-classes).
concrete class: A class with no pure virtual functions (every inherited one overridden), which can be instantiated. Needs a virtual destructor if it is a base class with children. See [Interfaces and the virtual destructor](#/comp3522-w4/interfaces).
interface: A pure abstract class: only pure virtual functions, a regular virtual destructor, no data members; describes behaviour without any implementation. Java's `interface` / `implements`. See [Interfaces and the virtual destructor](#/comp3522-w4/interfaces).
virtual destructor: `virtual ~Animal() {}` in a base class, so that `delete` through a base pointer runs the derived class's destructor first. Without it only the base destructor runs: undefined behaviour and leaked members. See [Interfaces and the virtual destructor](#/comp3522-w4/interfaces).
override: Keyword on a derived function asking the compiler to check that it overrides a virtual function with the same signature; an error if the base function is not virtual. See [Pure virtual functions and abstract classes](#/comp3522-w4/abstract-classes).
multiple inheritance: A class with more than one base class, `class C : public A, public B`; its members are the union of the bases' members, and same-named members become ambiguous. See [Multiple inheritance and ambiguity](#/comp3522-w4/multiple-inheritance).
ambiguous|ambiguously inherited: A member that two bases both provide, so the derived class cannot use it unqualified (`bob.all_info()` is an error); resolve with `bob.mathematician::all_info()` or an override. See [Multiple inheritance and ambiguity](#/comp3522-w4/multiple-inheritance).
using person::person: Inherits the base class's constructors into the derived class, equivalent to writing a forwarding constructor for each. See [Multiple inheritance and ambiguity](#/comp3522-w4/multiple-inheritance).
diamond: The hierarchy where two classes derive from the same base and a fourth derives from both: person, student and mathematician, math_student. Without virtual bases the bottom class holds two copies of the top one. See [The diamond and virtual base classes](#/comp3522-w4/diamond-virtual-base).
virtual base class|virtual base|public v: Declared with `class student : public virtual person` in every middle class, so the most derived object holds one shared person instead of one per path. See [The diamond and virtual base classes](#/comp3522-w4/diamond-virtual-base).
most derived class: The class at the bottom of the diamond (math_student). With virtual bases it is responsible for calling the shared base's constructor, `: person(name), student(passed), mathematician(proved)`; the middle classes' calls to `person(...)` are ignored. See [The diamond and virtual base classes](#/comp3522-w4/diamond-virtual-base).
friend: A declaration inside a class body that grants a function (`friend Dollar sum(...)`) or a whole class (`friend class Spy;`) access to its private and protected members. The definition lives outside the class; friendship is not mutual, not transitive, not inherited, and the access specifier around it is irrelevant. See [Friend functions and friend classes](#/comp3522-w4/friends).
operator overloading: Defining a function with a special name such as `operator+=` or `operator<<` so that an operator works on operands of a user-defined type; 38 operators can be overloaded. See [Operator overloading: the canonical forms](#/comp3522-w4/operator-overloading).
operator<<: The insertion operator, the most commonly overloaded: `friend ostream& operator<<(ostream& os, const T& obj) { os << ...; return os; }`, a friendly non-member because its left operand is a stream. See [Operator overloading: the canonical forms](#/comp3522-w4/operator-overloading).
operator>>: The extraction operator: `friend istream& operator>>(istream& is, T& obj) { is >> obj.x; return is; }`; the object is a non-const reference because it is filled in. See [Operator overloading: the canonical forms](#/comp3522-w4/operator-overloading).
operator++: Prefix `Counter& operator++()` increments and returns `*this`; postfix `Counter operator++(int)` takes a dummy int, copies the original, calls prefix, and returns the copy (slower). Both are members. See [Operator overloading: the canonical forms](#/comp3522-w4/operator-overloading).
operator+=: Member function that adds to the left operand and returns `*this` by reference; `operator+` is a friendly non-member that copies its left operand, calls `+=`, and returns the copy. See [Operator overloading: the canonical forms](#/comp3522-w4/operator-overloading).
operator+: Friendly non-member `friend Fraction operator+(Fraction lhs, const Fraction& rhs) { lhs += rhs; return lhs; }`: returns a new value and leaves the operands unchanged; being a non-member also allows `5 + a`. See [Operator overloading: the canonical forms](#/comp3522-w4/operator-overloading).
operator<|operator==|operator!=|operator: The six comparison operators, all friendly non-members; write `==` and `<`, then `!=` is `!(lhs == rhs)`, `>` is `rhs < lhs`, `<=` is `!(lhs > rhs)`, `>=` is `!(lhs < rhs)`. The standard library expects `operator<`. See [Operator overloading: the canonical forms](#/comp3522-w4/operator-overloading).
copy assignment operator|operator=: The member `MyClass& operator=(MyClass rhs)` that runs for `B = A;` when both objects already exist. The canonical form is copy-and-swap: swap `*this` with the by-value copy and `return *this;`. See [The copy assignment operator and copy-and-swap](#/comp3522-w4/copy-assignment).
copy-and-swap|copy and swap: The idiom behind the canonical `operator=`: the by-value parameter is built by the copy constructor, a swap function exchanges every member with it, and the temporary's destructor frees the old data when the function ends. Needs a copy constructor, a destructor and a non-throwing swap. See [The copy assignment operator and copy-and-swap](#/comp3522-w4/copy-assignment).
mySwap|swap: The member-by-member swap used by copy-and-swap: `using std::swap; swap(first.size, second.size); swap(first.my_list, second.my_list);`. Never `std::swap` the whole object (it would call `operator=` again). See [The copy assignment operator and copy-and-swap](#/comp3522-w4/copy-assignment).
rule of three: A class that owns a resource through a pointer needs its own copy constructor, destructor and copy assignment operator, because the compiler's versions copy the pointer. See [The copy assignment operator and copy-and-swap](#/comp3522-w4/copy-assignment).
memory leak: Heap memory with no pointer left to it, so it can never be deleted; caused by `i = a;` before `delete i;`. Prevent with one delete per new, deleting before re-pointing, and destructors in owning classes. See [Midterm practice questions, worked](#/comp3522-w4/midterm-practice).
